passage_title: Let the Schoolyard Hold the Rain
student_passage:
Let the Schoolyard Hold the Rain

[1] Any change to a schoolyard must preserve safe routes for play, arrival, and emergency access. [2] During heavy rain, broad paved schoolyards can send water rapidly toward crowded street drains. [3] Schools should replace carefully selected sections of pavement with shallow rain gardens.[1] A site-specific design can satisfy the safety requirement while allowing part of the grounds to slow and absorb runoff.

A rain garden is a planted depression rather than a permanent pond. Soil and gravel beneath the plants spawn[2] temporary storage space for water that would otherwise cross the pavement. Planted in a shallow basin, runoff can spread among grasses and flowering perennials.[3] The basin drains after a storm, leaving the area ready to collect water again.

Several small gardens can serve different portions of a large schoolyard. The gardens direct water through its[4] curb openings and overflow paths. In addition,[5] students can compare rainfall with the time each basin takes to drain, turning routine maintenance into an opportunity for observation. Science classes might identify pollinators, measure plant growth, or examine how soil texture affects infiltration.

[A] Administrators may reasonably worry that a garden will become neglected after its first year. [B] The design should therefore include durable native plants, a defined path, and access for removing litter. [C] A rotating class or garden club can inspect the site after major storms. [D] A written maintenance calendar would make responsibility visible before enthusiasm for the new project fades.[6] A small oversight team that meet[7] each month can record blocked inlets, damaged plants, and repairs.

No school should remove pavement merely to claim that it has built a rain garden. A basin placed where water never flows would be a laughably terrible waste that makes absolutely no sense[8]. Before construction, planners should verify three conditions; the direction of runoff, the rate at which soil drains, and the space needed for existing school activities[9]. A well-sited rain garden can manage water, support instruction, and improve a schoolyard precisely because its environmental purpose is joined to an operating plan.[10]
